raw_content:
{
  "hook": "100% Syrah in Gigondas is a legal oddity—the appellation normally forces Grenache to lead—so des Bosquets’ ‘Les Routes’ tastes like a Northern Rhône exile that woke up under Provençal sun. The wine carries the black-pepper snap and smoked-meat savor you expect from Saint-Joseph, but the limestone scree of the Dentelles pumps it with warmer blackberry and a garrigue scrub that screams southern France.",
  "wine_summary": "Domaine des Bosquets farms biodynamically on the upper slopes of the Dentelles de Montmirail, where poor, rocky limestone soils force low yields and thick-skinned berries. By bottling a mono-varietal Syrah they step outside the appellation’s Grenache-driven norm, proving Gigondas can speak with a northern accent while keeping its southern muscle. The estate’s 40-60 year old Syrah parcels sit at 350–450 m, catching the cool dusk drainage that slides off the jagged peaks; that altitude plus the limestone bedrock keeps alcohol in check and infuses the wine with a stony snap rarely found in the flat-valley Grenache blends that dominate the village.",
  "terroir_expression": "Decomposed limestone scree and thin marl on the Dentelles’ slopes heat up by day, then radiate warmth after sunset while the cool mistral sweeps away moisture; this diurnal swing lets Syrah ripen to 14.5% without losing its peppery rotundone. The limestone’s high pH lowers available nitrogen, slowing fermentation and preserving the grape’s violet top note, while the rocky topsoil limits water retention, shrinking berries and thickening skins—source of the wine’s ink-black color and iron-fisted tannins that taste like crushed stone and tapenade.",
  "vinification_summary": "Whole-cluster fermentation (about 40%) adds stem tannin and amplifies the black-pepper rotundone; native yeasts, no added acid, and a gentle 24-day maceration keep the savory edge. The wine rests 18 months: 70% in 600-L demi-muid (neutral French oak, 4-6 years old) and 30% raw concrete egg—the larger format softens tannin without vanilla sweetness, while concrete’s micro-oxygenation polishes texture yet preserves the limestone-driven mineral cut.",
  "food_pairing": "Nashville hot chicken on white bread—the wine’s cracked-pepper spice and limestone tannin scrub the cayenne oil clean while its dark fruit cools the burn. Herb-crusted lamb saddle with black-olive tapenade mirrors the wine’s olive-and-herb savor and salty finish. For Paris bistro night, steak-frites béarnaise: the Syrah’s pepper and acidity slice through buttery hollandaise, and the limestone snap refreshes between fries. Vegetarians: char-grilled portobello layered with smoked goat cheese—the wine’s meaty smoke plays off the mushroom’s umami while acidity tackles the cheese.",
  "comparable_wines": "Saint-Joseph ‘Les Vins de Vienne’ 2020 — same 100% Syrah, granite instead of limestone, so more bacon-fat smoke yet similar pepper and violet. Château Pesquié ‘Artemia’ Syrah, Ventoux — limestone foothills of Mont Ventoux just southwest, warmer fruit but shared garrigue herbs. Tablas Creek Syrah, Paso Robles Adelaida District — chalky limestone soils transplanted from Beaucastel, giving Californian sun fruit with a similar stony cut.",
  "style_profile": "Full-bodied dry Syrah with iron-firm tannins, black-pepper spice and limestone-driven mineral snap",
  "cellar_recommendation": "Drink 2026-2032; ten-year window if you like the savory olive phase, though fruit peaks around year seven. Store 12°C/54°F, 70% humidity—limestone tannins need slow oxygen so leave the Diam cork horizontal.",
  "value_assessment": "Around $45-50 US puts it head-to-head with Saint-Joseph at the same price but delivers an extra half-point of body; you’re paying $10 less than Châteauneuf of equal score and getting more acid lift. Competes directly with Alain Graillot Saint-Joseph (similar sticker) yet gives you southern Rhône ripeness—worth it if you want pepper without the Northern Rhône price bump.",
  "market_position": "Shows up on progressive Paris wine-bar lists (Septime, Le Mary Celeste) and in U.S. indie retail bins where staff push ‘odd-ball cuvées’ to geek clientele hunting Northern Rhône character below the Émérité tax bracket. Doesn’t appear in supermarket Rhône sets—Gigondas shelves are Grenache-heavy—so buyers are either Syrah purists or collectors chasing legal outliers.",
  "insider_take": "Skip this if you’re chasing the plush, kirsch-bomb Gigondas that critics score on glycerol—this wine is angular, crackling, and needs protein or time. Buy it precisely because the appellation makes it an orphan: it’s Saint-Joseph in disguise wearing southern alcohol, and pricing hasn’t caught up to the sleight of hand.",

  "drinking_window_min_years": 3,
  "drinking_window_max_years": 12,

parsed.insider_take: Skip this if you’re chasing the plush, kirsch-bomb Gigondas that critics score on glycerol—this wine is angular, crackling, and needs protein or time. Buy it precisely because the appellation makes it an orphan: it’s Saint-Joseph in disguise wearing southern alcohol, and pricing hasn’t caught up to the sleight of hand.
